# Chapter 4 Practice: Reactions in Aqueous Solution

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/aqueous-reactions.md`), grouped by objective. 27 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats. Within each objective the questions run from easier to harder.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 4.1a}} · *multiple-choice* A solution conducts electricity because it contains

A. dissolved molecules
B. free ions
C. a large amount of solute
D. water
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** Electric current is moving charge, so the solution must contain charged particles free to move. Neutral dissolved molecules cannot carry a current no matter how many there are.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 4.1a}} · *short answer* Classify each as a strong electrolyte, weak electrolyte, or nonelectrolyte: $\ce{NaNO3}$, $\ce{HF}$, sucrose, $\ce{HCl}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
- $\ce{NaNO3}$ — a soluble ionic salt: **strong electrolyte**.
- $\ce{HF}$ — hydrofluoric acid is a weak acid: **weak electrolyte**.
- Sucrose — a molecular compound that dissolves without ionizing: **nonelectrolyte**.
- $\ce{HCl}$ — one of the seven strong acids: **strong electrolyte**.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 4.1a}} · *short answer* Explain why solid $\ce{NaCl}$ does not conduct electricity but a solution of $\ce{NaCl}$ does.
:::
::: tab Answer
Both contain ions, so the presence of ions is not the whole story — **mobility** is.

In the solid, the $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions are locked into fixed positions in the crystal lattice and cannot move. When the solid dissolves, water molecules surround each ion (hydration) and pull the lattice apart, leaving the ions free to move through the solution and carry current.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 4.1a}} · *short answer* A 0.10 M solution of acetic acid conducts electricity much more weakly than a 0.10 M solution of HCl, even though both contain the same concentration of acid. Explain.
:::
::: tab Answer
The comparison is between how much acid was *added* and how many ions actually *exist*.

HCl is a strong acid, so essentially all of it ionizes: a 0.10 M solution contains close to 0.10 M $\ce{H+}$ and 0.10 M $\ce{Cl-}$.

Acetic acid is weak and ionizes only slightly — the great majority stays as intact $\ce{CH3COOH}$ molecules, so the ion concentration is a small fraction of 0.10 M. Fewer charge carriers means weaker conduction.

"Strong" and "weak" describe the *extent of ionization*, not the concentration.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 4.2a}} · *short answer* Predict whether each is soluble in water: $\ce{NaOH}$, $\ce{CaCO3}$, $\ce{NH4Cl}$, $\ce{PbSO4}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
- $\ce{NaOH}$ — hydroxides are usually insoluble, but sodium is Group 1A and that rule always wins: **soluble**.
- $\ce{CaCO3}$ — a carbonate without a Group 1A cation or ammonium: **insoluble**.
- $\ce{NH4Cl}$ — ammonium compounds are always soluble: **soluble**.
- $\ce{PbSO4}$ — most sulfates are soluble, but lead(II) sulfate is one of the insoluble ones: **insoluble**.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 4.2a}} · *short answer* Solutions of $\ce{Pb(NO3)2}$ and $\ce{KI}$ are mixed. Predict whether a precipitate forms, and identify it.
:::
::: tab Answer
Work out the two possible new pairings: $\ce{PbI2}$ and $\ce{KNO3}$.

$\ce{KNO3}$ — potassium is Group 1A and nitrate is always soluble, so this stays dissolved.

$\ce{PbI2}$ — iodides are mostly soluble, but lead(II) iodide is a well-known exception.

**A precipitate forms: $\ce{PbI2}$**, the bright yellow solid this reaction is famous for.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 4.2b}} · *workout* Write the molecular, ionic, and net ionic equations for the reaction between $\ce{BaCl2(aq)}$ and $\ce{Na2SO4(aq)}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Molecular.** The new pairings are $\ce{BaSO4}$ (the memorized insoluble sulfate) and $\ce{NaCl}$ (soluble):
$$\ce{BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}$$

**Ionic.** Split every strong electrolyte; the solid stays whole:
$$\ce{Ba^2+ + 2Cl- + 2Na+ + SO4^2- -> BaSO4(s) + 2Na+ + 2Cl-}$$

**Net ionic.** Cancel the spectators $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$:
$$\ce{Ba^2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s)}$$

Check: charge $(+2)+(-2)=0$ on both sides. ✓
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 4.2b}} · *short answer* Identify the spectator ions when $\ce{AgNO3(aq)}$ reacts with $\ce{KCl(aq)}$, and explain what makes an ion a spectator.
:::
::: tab Answer
The reaction forms insoluble $\ce{AgCl}$, so the net ionic equation is $\ce{Ag+ + Cl- -> AgCl(s)}$.

The **spectator ions are $\ce{K+}$ and $\ce{NO3-}$.**

An ion is a spectator when it is present in exactly the same form — dissolved and unchanged — on both sides of the ionic equation. It was in solution before and it is in solution after, so it took no part in the chemistry and cancels.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 4.2b}} · *workout* Solutions of $\ce{NaCl}$ and $\ce{KNO3}$ are mixed. Write the net ionic equation.
:::
::: tab Answer
The possible new pairings are $\ce{NaNO3}$ and $\ce{KCl}$. Both sodium and potassium are Group 1A, and nitrate is always soluble, so **both pairings are soluble**.

No precipitate forms, every ion is a spectator, and **there is no net ionic equation** — no reaction occurs.

Recognizing the no-reaction case is part of the skill: a precipitation reaction requires one of the *new* pairings to be insoluble.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 4.3a}} · *multiple-choice* According to the Brønsted definition, an acid is

A. a substance that produces $\ce{OH-}$ in water
B. a proton acceptor
C. a proton donor
D. any substance that tastes sour
:::
::: tab Answer
**C.** A Brønsted acid donates a proton ($\ce{H+}$); a Brønsted base accepts one. Option A describes an Arrhenius base.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 4.3a}} · *short answer* Classify each as a strong or weak acid: $\ce{HBr}$, $\ce{CH3COOH}$, $\ce{H2SO4}$, $\ce{HNO2}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
- $\ce{HBr}$ — **strong** (on the list of seven).
- $\ce{CH3COOH}$ — **weak**; it contains the $\ce{-COOH}$ group, and every acid with that group is weak.
- $\ce{H2SO4}$ — **strong**, though only on its first proton; the $\ce{HSO4-}$ that remains is weak.
- $\ce{HNO2}$ — **weak**. Note the contrast with $\ce{HNO3}$, which is strong. One oxygen atom separates them.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 4.3a}} · *short answer* In $\ce{NH3 + H2O <=> NH4+ + OH-}$, identify the Brønsted acid and base in the forward direction and in the reverse direction.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Forward:** $\ce{H2O}$ donates a proton to $\ce{NH3}$, so **water is the acid** and **ammonia is the base**.

**Reverse:** $\ce{NH4+}$ donates a proton to $\ce{OH-}$, so **the ammonium ion is the acid** and **hydroxide is the base**.

Water acts as an acid here and as a base in other reactions. Under the Brønsted definition, acid and base are roles in a particular reaction, not fixed labels.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 4.3b}} · *workout* Write the net ionic equation for $\ce{HNO3(aq) + KOH(aq) -> KNO3(aq) + H2O}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Nitric acid is strong, potassium hydroxide is a strong base, and potassium nitrate is soluble — so all three split:
$$\ce{H+ + NO3- + K+ + OH- -> K+ + NO3- + H2O}$$

Canceling the spectators $\ce{K+}$ and $\ce{NO3-}$:
$$\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 4.3b}} · *workout* Write the net ionic equation for $\ce{HF(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaF(aq) + H2O}$, and explain why it differs from Q13's.
:::
::: tab Answer
$\ce{HF}$ is a **weak** acid, so it stays as intact molecules:
$$\ce{HF + Na+ + OH- -> Na+ + F- + H2O}$$

Only $\ce{Na+}$ is a spectator:
$$\ce{HF + OH- -> F- + H2O}$$

It differs from Q13 because the acid is weak. A strong acid is already fully split into $\ce{H+}$ before it meets the base, so every strong-acid/strong-base neutralization collapses to $\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}$. A weak acid still has its proton attached, so the acid itself must appear in the equation.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 4.3b}} · *workout* Write the net ionic equation for $\ce{H2SO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) -> Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Sulfuric acid is strong, sodium hydroxide is strong, sodium sulfate is soluble:
$$\ce{2H+ + SO4^2- + 2Na+ + 2OH- -> 2Na+ + SO4^2- + 2H2O}$$

Cancel $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{SO4^2-}$:
$$\ce{2H+ + 2OH- -> 2H2O}$$

Then reduce to lowest whole-number coefficients:
$$\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}$$

Forgetting the final reduction is the usual slip here.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 4.4a}} · *workout* Determine the oxidation number of the specified element: (a) S in $\ce{H2SO4}$; (b) Mn in $\ce{MnO4-}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) S in $\ce{H2SO4}$.** H is $+1$ (two of them), O is $-2$ (four of them), and the molecule is neutral:
$$2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x = +6$$

**(b) Mn in $\ce{MnO4-}$.** Four oxygens give $-8$, and the ion's charge is $-1$:
$$x + 4(-2) = -1 \;\Rightarrow\; x = +7$$

The only difference between the two is what the sum must equal: zero for a neutral molecule, the ion's charge for an ion.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 4.4a}} · *workout* Determine the oxidation number of oxygen in $\ce{H2O}$ and in $\ce{H2O2}$, and explain the difference.
:::
::: tab Answer
**In $\ce{H2O}$:** $2(+1) + x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -2$, the usual value.

**In $\ce{H2O2}$:** $2(+1) + 2x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1$.

$\ce{H2O2}$ is a **peroxide**, the named exception to the "oxygen is $-2$" rule. Peroxides contain an oxygen–oxygen bond, and a bond between two atoms of the same element contributes nothing to either atom's oxidation number, so each oxygen ends up at $-1$ rather than $-2$.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 4.4a}} · *short answer* For $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$, identify what is oxidized, what is reduced, and name both agents.
:::
::: tab Answer
Assign oxidation numbers to each element on both sides:

- Fe: $+3$ in $\ce{Fe2O3}$ → $0$ as the free metal. It went **down**, so iron was **reduced**.
- C: $+2$ in $\ce{CO}$ → $+4$ in $\ce{CO2}$. It went **up**, so carbon was **oxidized**.
- O stays at $-2$ throughout and takes no part.

Therefore $\ce{Fe2O3}$ is the **oxidizing agent** (it was reduced) and $\ce{CO}$ is the **reducing agent** (it was oxidized).

This is the blast-furnace reaction that produces most of the world's iron.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 4.4b}} · *short answer* Classify each: (a) $\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}$; (b) $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$; \(c) $\ce{Cl2 + 2NaBr -> 2NaCl + Br2}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) Combination** (also a combustion, since $\ce{O2}$ is a reactant). Two reactants become one product.

**(b) Decomposition.** One compound becomes two simpler ones. It is also a **disproportionation**: oxygen starts at $-1$ in the peroxide and ends at both $-2$ (in water) and $0$ (as $\ce{O2}$) — the same element both oxidized and reduced.

**\(c) Halogen displacement.** Chlorine is more active than bromine ($\ce{F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2}$), so it displaces bromide from the compound.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 4.4b}} · *short answer* Using the activity series, predict whether each occurs: (a) $\ce{Ag}$ in $\ce{HCl(aq)}$; (b) $\ce{Mg}$ in $\ce{HCl(aq)}$; \(c) $\ce{Cu}$ in $\ce{AgNO3(aq)}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a) No.** Silver sits in the bottom tier and does not release $\ce{H2}$ from water or acid.

**(b) Yes.** Magnesium is well above hydrogen in activity: $\ce{Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2}$.

**\(c) Yes.** Copper is more active than silver, so it displaces silver from solution: $\ce{Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag}$. Silver metal deposits as visible crystals.

Note that copper failed in (a) against acid but succeeds in \(c) against silver. Activity is always a comparison — the question is not "is this metal reactive?" but "is it more reactive than the thing it would have to displace?"
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 4.4b}} · *short answer* Give an example of a disproportionation reaction and show why it qualifies.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\ce{Cl2 + 2OH- -> ClO- + Cl- + H2O}$$

Chlorine begins as the free element, oxidation number **0**. In the products it appears twice: at **$+1$** in $\ce{ClO-}$ (where oxygen is $-2$ and the ion charge is $-1$) and at **$-1$** in $\ce{Cl-}$.

The same element was simultaneously oxidized ($0 \to +1$) and reduced ($0 \to -1$), which is what disproportionation means. This reaction is how household bleach is made.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 4.5a}} · *workout* What is the molarity of a solution containing 0.250 mol of solute in 400.0 mL of solution?
:::
::: tab Answer
Convert the volume to liters, then divide:
$$M = \frac{0.250\ \text{mol}}{0.4000\ \text{L}} = 0.625\ \text{M}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 4.5a}} · *workout* How many grams of $\ce{KMnO4}$ (158.03 g/mol) are needed to prepare 500.0 mL of a 0.0400 M solution?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$0.5000\,\text{L}\times\frac{0.0400\,\text{mol}}{1\,\text{L}}\times\frac{158.03\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{mol}}=3.16\ \text{g}$$

In practice: weigh 3.16 g, dissolve it in some water, then add water until the total volume is exactly 500.0 mL.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 4.5a}} · *workout* What volume of 6.00 M $\ce{HNO3}$ is needed to prepare 250.0 mL of 0.500 M $\ce{HNO3}$?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$V_i=\frac{M_fV_f}{M_i}=\frac{0.500\,\text{M}\times250.0\,\text{mL}}{6.00\,\text{M}}=20.8\ \text{mL}$$

Measure 20.8 mL of the stock, then add water to a total volume of 250.0 mL.

Since the volumes appear as a ratio, both may stay in milliliters.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 25
{{sp[info] Objective 4.5b}} · *workout* What is the concentration of each ion in a 0.15 M solution of $\ce{Na3PO4}$?
:::
::: tab Answer
Write the dissociation first:
$$\ce{Na3PO4 -> 3Na+ + PO4^3-}$$

$$[\ce{Na+}] = 3\times0.15 = 0.45\ \text{M}\qquad [\ce{PO4^3-}] = 1\times0.15 = 0.15\ \text{M}$$

The label's 0.15 M refers to the compound. Only the phosphate happens to match it; the sodium is three times higher.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 26
{{sp[info] Objective 4.5b}} · *workout* It takes 35.0 mL of 0.200 M NaOH to neutralize 25.0 mL of an HCl solution. What is the HCl concentration?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\ce{HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O}\quad\text{(1:1)}$$

Moles of the known:
$$0.0350\,\text{L}\times0.200\,\text{M}=7.00\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol NaOH}$$

The 1:1 ratio gives $7.00\times10^{-3}$ mol HCl. Divide by the *acid's* volume:
$$M=\frac{7.00\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}}{0.0250\ \text{L}}=0.280\ \text{M}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 27
{{sp[info] Objective 4.5b}} · *workout* A 25.0 mL sample of $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$ requires 18.4 mL of 0.150 M HCl to reach the equivalence point. What is the $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$ concentration?
:::
::: tab Answer
The balanced equation decides everything, and $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$ supplies **two** hydroxides:
$$\ce{Ba(OH)2 + 2HCl -> BaCl2 + 2H2O}$$

Moles of the known:
$$0.0184\,\text{L}\times0.150\,\text{M}=2.76\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol HCl}$$

Cross with the 1:2 ratio:
$$2.76\times10^{-3}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Ba(OH)2}}{2\,\text{mol HCl}}=1.38\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$$

$$M=\frac{1.38\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}}{0.0250\ \text{L}}=0.0552\ \text{M}$$

Assuming 1:1 would give 0.110 M, twice the correct value. Write the balanced equation before the arithmetic.
:::
::::
